title: The animals
hook: he told of a sinner forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the children, and a prayer that waited for a boy. Your line was the child on his back. Did a child slow you down, and did you let them? Day two hundred seventy-two.

A man is walking a desert road on a brutally hot day, and he's desperate for water. He finds a well, climbs down into it, drinks, and climbs back up. And there, at the top, is a dog. Panting, tongue out, so thirsty it's licking the damp mud around the well. The man thinks: this dog is feeling exactly what I was feeling a minute ago. He has no bucket. He has no cup. What would you do? Walk on? It's a dog, and you've had your drink. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told this story to his companions, and the ending surprised them so much they had to ask him a question. Today: the animals.
screen: `A DESERT ROAD, A WELL.` → `A DOG LICKING THE MUD.` → `NO BUCKET, NO CUP.`

segments.voice: The man climbed back down the well. He filled his leather sock with water, held it in his teeth so he could use both hands to climb, came up, and gave the dog a drink. And the Prophet said, in the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari: God thanked him for it, and forgave him. The companions asked: messenger of God, is there really a reward for us in animals? And he answered with a line Muslims still quote: in every living creature there is reward. Another version of the story, also in Bukhari, makes it even sharper: the one who gave the water was a woman known for sin, and she was forgiven for it. And the Prophet told the other side too. A woman locked up a cat, didn't feed it, and didn't let it go to find food, until it died, and he said she was punished for it. The same care shows up in the stories of his own life. Companions on a journey once took two chicks from a bird's nest, and the mother bird circled over them in distress. The Prophet asked, who has troubled this bird by taking her young? Give them back to her. And one day in a garden in Medina a camel saw him and moaned, with tears in its eyes. He went to it, stroked it until it calmed, then found its owner and told him: don't you fear God concerning this animal? It has told me you starve it and wear it out. The Qur'an says that every creature on earth and every bird on two wings are communities, like you.
screen: `WATER IN HIS LEATHER SOCK.` · `IN EVERY LIVING CREATURE, REWARD.` · `GIVE THE BIRD HER YOUNG.` · `COMMUNITIES, LIKE YOU.` · then, large: `WATER FOR THE DOG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put out water for an animal. If you can, do it now, or plan it: a bowl on the step, a dish in the yard, fresh water for a pet whose bowl you haven't checked. Then sit, and think about the animals near you that you mostly don't notice. Birds on the wire. A neighbor's dog. The cat in the alley. Picture each one, for a moment, as a community of its own. The bell holds the time.
The animals. The Prophet's teaching that there's reward in every living creature, from a thirsty dog to a grieving bird. Today's word.
Your line: water for the dog. Today, do one kind thing for an animal, even a small one, and remember it counts. Day two hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Many Muslims leave water out for birds and stray animals, especially in hot weather, citing the hadith of the thirsty dog, and Islamic law has long set out duties of care toward working and domestic animals.

fork.setup: you've climbed out of a well after drinking. a dog is dying of thirst at the top. you have no bucket. what do you do?
options: walk on. it's only a dog.
climb back down and bring water in your sock.
call for someone else to help it.
fork.reveal: he climbed down, filled his leather sock, carried it in his teeth, and watered the dog. God thanked him and forgave him.

original.note: Arabic: in every moist liver there is reward, meaning every living creature.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to animals.
what it means: a sinner forgiven for watering a dog: in every living creature, there is reward.
what a scholar hears: the Arabic says in every moist liver, an idiom for anything alive; jurists built rules on animal welfare from these hadith.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2363 (the man and the thirsty dog; in every living creature there is reward)

Sunan Abi Dawud 2675 (the bird and her chicks); 2549 (the camel)
Qur'an 6:38 (animals and birds are communities like you)

notes: The outline says 'a sinner'; Bukhari 2363 has a man, 3467 a woman prostitute of the Children of Israel. Both mentioned; confirm tone.
The camel story (Abu Dawud 2549) includes the camel 'complaining' to the Prophet; told as the hadith tells it.
